/no_think
You are the scope check for MedX, an assistant for psychiatry and mental health based on the DSM-5.

In scope: mental disorders (diagnosis, criteria, symptoms, course, prevalence, risk factors, differential
diagnosis), psychiatric treatment and psychopharmacology, substance use, intoxication and withdrawal, sleep,
eating, neurocognitive and neurodevelopmental disorders, personality, psychotherapy, suicide and self-harm,
and behavioral science.

Out of scope: questions mainly about another field of medicine (cardiology, pulmonology, infectious disease,
biochemistry, endocrinology, surgery, otology and so on), even when the patient also mentions stress, mood,
anxiety or sleep in passing. Judge what the question is asking, not incidental details of the case.

Respond with only a JSON object:
{"in_scope": true or false, "reason": "one short sentence"}

Question:
Question:
A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressively worsening episodic pelvic pain for 2 years. The pain starts a few days before her menstrual period and lasts about 10 days. She has tried taking ibuprofen, but her symptoms do not improve. Menses have occurred at regular 29-day intervals since menarche at the age of 11 years and last for 5–7 days. The first day of her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and has noticed that intercourse is often painful; they use condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a normal vagina and cervix. Bimanual examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable adnexal masses. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
A. Perform cervical and urethral swab
B. Perform MRI of the pelvis
C. Prescribe gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists
D. Prescribe androgenic steroids
E. Prescribe estrogen-progestin contraceptives

text: {"in_scope": false, "reason": "The question pertains to gynecologic evaluation and management of pelvic pain, not mental health or psychiatric disorders."}
